ask.question: What models are compared, and which performs best?
ask.answer: In this study, five machine learning models are compared: CNN, SVM, Gradient Boosting, MLP, and Random Forest. The model that performs best is the CNN, as evidenced by its accuracy of 96%, precision, recall, and F1-score for both the "fresh" and "rotten" classes, and the highest AUC of 0.995 in the ROC curve comparison [1], [2], [5].

ask.question: What datasets do these papers use, and how large are they?
ask.answer: [1] and [5] use datasets for different purposes. [1] uses MuReD, RFMiD, and RFMiD 2.0 datasets, with MuReD being the preferred dataset for reproducing the C- Tran paper. MuReD contains 2208 labels in total, split into 1766 for training, 442 for validation, and 20 for testing. [5] uses a mouse early gastrulation scRNA-seq dataset, which was generated from seven chimeric E8.5 embryos of WT and Tal1 KO cells. The dataset size is not explicitly stated, but it is mentioned that the data were normalized and processed in a way similar to the Paul et al. dataset.

ask.question: What limitations do the authors state about their own work?
ask.answer: The authors state that their work is constrained by data size and class imbalances, which could lead to randomness and potential overfitting [4]. Additionally, they highlight that the input data may not report the emergence of new transcriptional states in the context of loss of gene function, suggesting that existing single-cell data supports the use of CellOracle to accurately simulate TF perturbation effects [3]. They also note that the method has limitations, such as the inability to analyze cell states that do not exist in the input scRNA-seq data and the limitation by input data availability and quality [3]. Furthermore, they acknowledge that their models were not tuned for hyperparameters, which may affect their performance in real-world applications [1]. Lastly, they mention that their models were only evaluated based on standard metrics like accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, which do not account for real-time performance or model robustness under different conditions such as noise or varying data distributions [1].

summary.title: Retinal Fundus Multi-Disease Image Classification using Hybrid CNN-Transformer-Ensemble Architectures

fields.name: research_problem
fields.label: Research problem
fields.value: Our research addresses the urgent global issue of a large population affected by retinal diseases, which are unevenly distributed and underserved by specialized medical expertise, particularly in non-urban areas. The primary objective is to bridge this healthcare gap by developing a comprehensive diagnostic system capable of accurately predicting retinal diseases from fundus images.

fields.name: contribution
fields.label: Main contribution
fields.value: Our work introduces six novel models that combine deeper CNN backbones, transformer encoders, and ensemble architectures. These models outperform baseline models, achieving a remarkable model score of 0.9166, surpassing the baseline score of 0.9. We also highlight the importance of domain knowledge in identifying relevant image regions and the use of the IEViT concept to improve transformer-based learning.

fields.name: data
fields.label: Data
fields.value: The paper chose the MuReD dataset for its relevance and utilization in the C- Tran paper, which was aimed at establishing baselines for the model. Future analysis will incorporate the RFMiD 2.0 and JSIEC datasets, which are the latest and encompass all essential labels of MuReD.

fields.name: methodology
fields.label: Methodology
fields.value: The authors applied various augmentation techniques to the dataset, including Random Horizontal Flip, to increase the diversity and variability of the training dataset. They also used Weighted Random Sampling and LP-ROS (10%) to address class imbalance, and utilized DenseNet121 and DenseNet201 as backbone models with ResNet152d for feature extraction. The IEViT concept was incorporated into the IeECT model to retain knowledge of the original image while maintaining fewer parameters.

fields.name: experimental_setup
fields.label: Experimental setup
fields.value: The study utilized the MuReD dataset, which is a refined variant of the highly imbalanced RFMiD dataset. The authors explored various deep CNN architectures as backbone models, including ResNet152d, DenseNet121, DenseNet201, and EfficientNetV2Small, and used these models as feature extractors. They also applied augmentation techniques and addressed class imbalance using Weighted Random Sampling and LP-ROS (10%). The IEViT concept was used in the IeECT model to ensure the model retained knowledge of the original image while maintaining fewer parameters.

fields.name: results
fields.label: Results
fields.value: The results demonstrated that the proposed hybrid models, including the ensemble models with deeper CNN backbones and the ensemble variant 2 with a single transformer layer, outperformed the baseline models. Specifically, the ensemble variant 1 achieved a model score above 0.91, surpassing the baseline in 5 out of 8 metrics. The ROC curve for the Ensemble model is shown in Fig. 3, and the comparative performance is detailed in Table 6, which indicates that the proposed models outperformed the state-of-the-art model with a score of 0.9. Additionally, the IEViT v2 DPD variant showed superior performance compared to the C-Tran baseline model while maintaining lower computational complexity.

fields.name: limitations
fields.label: Limitations
fields.value: The constraints imposed by data size and class imbalances could lead to randomness and potential overfitting, as highlighted in the paper. These challenges necessitate further refinement, particularly in improving model interpretability to enhance practical utility.

fields.name: future_work
fields.label: Future work
fields.value: Future work will focus on exploring the integration of Shapley values to make the model predictions more transparent and understandable. Additionally, the research aims to incorporate the RFMiD 2.0 and JSIEC datasets for a more comprehensive analysis, and the integration of Shapley values to make the model predictions more transparent and understandable.

MuReD, a refined variant of the highly imbalanced RFMiD dataset, was preferred due to its relevance.
